practicalQuestion: What should pre-training fueling and hydration prioritize for a collegiate athlete completing an early-morning high-intensity session when appetite is low and less than 45 minutes are available before training?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athletes participating in high-intensity morning training
decisionContext.phase: Before an early-morning field or court session
decisionContext.outcome: Support session quality with a practical, tolerable intake approach
decisionContext.constraints: Low appetite; limited preparation time; individual gastrointestinal tolerance; no clinical nutrition condition

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests fueling or hydration in the last 45 minutes before training, low morning appetite, or collegiate athletes. The closest evidence is review-level timing guidance that assumes longer windows (1 to 4 hours for carbohydrate, about 1 hour for caffeine). There is also observational hydration data from male American football practices. All of it is indirect for this decision.

dimensions.sourceReview: Four relevant sources were read in original text: two narrative reviews, one two-player case study, and two observational field studies. All are legacy or review records, and none is a trial of short-window pre-session intake.
dimensions.directness: Low. The timing guidance targets windows longer than 45 minutes and, for carbohydrate, competition rather than training. The hydration studies describe fluid balance and monitoring, not what to drink before a session.
dimensions.consistency: No material disagreement among sources, but they address different parts of the question and do not converge on a short-window approach.
dimensions.transferability: Limited. Populations were young professional male rugby league players, two elite male Australian football players, and male post-graduate and high school American football players. None were female or collegiate-specific, and no source addresses low appetite.

bottomLine.text: The library does not contain direct evidence on what to eat or drink in under 45 minutes when appetite is low. The available guidance places pre-exercise carbohydrate 1 to 4 hours before competition and caffeine about 1 hour before exercise, both longer than the time available here, and it comes from reviews in male athletes. Fluid balance varied widely between athletes in early-morning football practices. Hydration plans should therefore be individual, and urine checks alone did not reliably reflect body mass change.

actions.title: Option: a small, tolerable carbohydrate intake
actions.text: A narrative review suggests carbohydrate plus protein 1 to 4 hours before competition, scaled to body mass, and notes sport-specific data are thin. The evidence does not test intake inside 45 minutes or with low appetite. Any smaller, easier-to-tolerate intake in this window is professional judgment, not an evidence-based dose.

actions.title: Option: build carbohydrate availability before the morning
actions.text: In a case study of two elite male Australian football players, a 24-hour carbohydrate-loading protocol raised muscle glycogen to levels that appeared sufficient for match play. The evidence does not test whether prior-day or evening intake offsets a minimal pre-session intake before a morning training session.

actions.title: Option: caffeine only for athletes already using it
actions.text: Review guidance places caffeine about 1 hour before exercise, which is longer than this window. The response varies between individuals. Any use is an individual decision with the sports dietitian under applicable rules, not a default.

actions.title: Option: an individual fluid plan rather than a fixed volume
actions.text: Consensus cited in a field study recommends personalized hydration practices. In early-morning football practices, fluid balance ranged from loss to gain across athletes. The evidence does not test a specific pre-session drink volume for a short window.

monitoring.label: Pre and post session body mass
monitoring.text: In high school football players training in the heat, urine color and urine specific gravity did not significantly identify body mass changes. Body mass change gives more information than urine checks alone.

monitoring.label: Back-to-back sessions
monitoring.text: Body mass loss was significantly greater after two-a-day practices. Watch morning sessions that follow an evening or same-day session more closely.

monitoring.label: Tolerance and session quality log
monitoring.text: The evidence does not test gastrointestinal tolerance in a short pre-session window. As a professional caution, record what was taken, how it sat, and perceived session quality, and adjust individually.

guardrails.text: This brief informs staff judgment. It does not prescribe intake for any athlete. Doses quoted from reviews were developed for professional male rugby league players and general sport, not collegiate athletes in a 45-minute window.

The evidence does not address persistent low appetite. As a professional caution, refer recurring low appetite, weight change, or concern about low energy availability to the sports dietitian and medical team.
Do not judge hydration from urine color or specific gravity alone. These did not significantly detect body mass change in the studied players.

limitations.text: No source studies intake within 45 minutes of training or athletes with low appetite. The timing guidance found assumes about 1 to 4 hours.

Studied populations were male professional rugby league, elite male Australian football (two players), and male post-graduate and high school American football. Female and collegiate athletes are not represented.
Carbohydrate and caffeine guidance comes from narrative reviews whose authors note limited sport-specific data. The carbohydrate guidance targets competition rather than training.

whatCouldChange.text: Controlled studies of small pre-exercise carbohydrate or fluid intakes taken inside 45 minutes before high-intensity team-sport training, in collegiate men and women, would allow a direct recommendation.
Evidence on the gastrointestinal tolerance of different pre-session formats in athletes with low morning appetite could change which option is preferred.

evidence.excerpt: Competition nutrition should maximize glycogen availability by consuming 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate (∼80-320 g) plus 0.25 g/kg (∼20-30 g) protein, 1-4 hr preexercise for 80-120 kg players.

claims.text: The same review's authors state there may not be enough data to provide rugby league-specific nutrition recommendations.

claims.text: In a case study of two elite male Australian football forwards, a 24-hour carbohydrate-loading protocol (8 g/kg, with 2 g/kg in the prematch meal) raised muscle glycogen above 500 mmol/kg dw. The authors judged this level as appearing sufficient for elite match play demands.

Prematch CHO loading elevated muscle glycogen concentrations (ie, >500 mmol/kg dw), the magnitude of which appears sufﬁcient to meet the metabolic demands of elite AF match play.

claims.text: A narrative review reports that the current recommendation for caffeine supplementation is about 3 to 6 mg/kg taken about 1 hour before exercise.

evidence.excerpt: The current recommendation for caffeine supplementation is ingesting ~ 3-6 mg/kg about 1 h before the onset of exercise.

claims.text: The same review states that the performance response to caffeine varies between individuals and depends on the conditions of the exercise session.

evidence.excerpt: Overall, the performance response to caffeine and the effect of this substance on sleep quality can vary interindividually and depend on the conditions of the exercise session (time of onset, duration, etc.).

claims.text: In male American football athletes during early-morning outdoor pre-season practices, fluid balance varied substantially between athletes, from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain.

evidence.excerpt: Testing took place over the course of three pre-season outdoor practices held in the early mornings during 1 week in August.
Fluid balance also varied substantially among athletes; ranging from 2.35% loss to 0.47% gain during the practice sessions

claims.text: In male high school football players practicing in a hot environment, the sensitivity and specificity of urine color or urine specific gravity for determining body mass changes were not significant.

evidence.excerpt: Sensitivity and specificity for using Ucol or USG to determine BM changes was not significant.

claims.text: In the same high school football players, percent body mass loss was significantly greater after two-a-day practices.

evidence.excerpt: The %BM loss (%BML) was significantly greater (p 5 0.001 to 0.024) after 2-a-day practices.

assumptions: The session is a typical team-sport field or court session, not an extreme-heat event. Heat-specific cooling evidence in the pack was not applied.
The athlete has no clinical nutrition condition and is not under a separate medical nutrition plan, as stated in the context.
Any caffeine use would follow applicable athletics rules and sports dietitian oversight. The pack does not address these rules.
coverageGaps: No studies of carbohydrate, protein, or fluid intake taken within 45 minutes before high-intensity training.
No evidence on fueling strategies for athletes with low morning appetite or on gastrointestinal tolerance of pre-session formats.
No pre-training fueling or hydration evidence in collegiate or female team-sport athletes.
No evidence comparing liquid and solid pre-session options, or specific pre-session fluid volumes.
